notes.text: Then — When he was first called to his office.

I sanctified — I ordained thee for this public service. He speaks thus to Jeremiah, not to the other prophets, because he stood in need of greater encouragement than they, both in respect of the tenderness of his years, and the difficulties which he was to encounter with. The nations - To other nations besides the Jews.
Thou shalt speak — Fear not, I will make thee eloquent and courageous.
Then — God having excited the prophet by command and promise, now in a vision confirms him, either by the hand of an angel, or by himself in some visible shape.

The kingdoms — Having now received his commission, he is directed to whom he is to go; to the greatest, not only single persons, but whole nations, as the Babylonians, Persians, and Egyptians. To pull down - That is, to prophecy that I will pull down; which I will as certainly effect, as if thou hadst done it thyself: for, according to scripture-usage, the prophets are said to do that which they foretell shall come to pass. To plant - Metaphors taken from architects and gardeners: either the former words relate to the enemies of God, and the latter to his friends; or rather to both conditionally: if they repent, he will build them up, he will increase their families, and settle them in the land; if they do not, he will root them up, and pull them down.

glossa.text: *Before I formed thee.* Not that he existed before conception, as the heretics suspect; but because the Lord foreknew that he would be, he to whom the things to be done are already done; who calls those things which are not as those which are.

*Ah, ah, ah, Lord God.* He shrinks from an office which for his age he cannot sustain. With the same modesty with which Moses says that he is of a slender and thin voice; but the one, as being of great and sturdy age, is rebuked, while to this one, as to a boy, pardon is given, who is adorned with modesty and shame.

*And he sent,* etc. ((ID.)) It is to be noted that here the hand of God is sent, etc., *as far as* that he may receive confidence in preaching.

((ID.)) Upon four sad things two joyful ones follow, etc., *as far as* and he is bidden to give it to all the nations to drink.

*Unto the end.* ((AUG.)) Concerning the commendation of grace, etc., *as far as* grace is commended in almost every single syllable.

*Of the sons of Jonadab.* ((ID.)) To sons that are willing, etc., *as far as* who of themselves are evil.

((CAS.)) Or thus: we are admonished in the title to have the devotion of the sons of Jonadab, etc., *as far as* but they, by their accustomed malice, remained in obstinacy.

*In thee, O Lord, have I hoped.* The just man in general speaks, from the beginning of the world unto its end: placing all his hope in God, he commends his grace, lest we presume upon false things in ourselves.

((CAS.)) Or, the former captives are in the world, from which one can escape: the second in hell. Or, *of the former,* that is, of those who were taken by vices before they became sons of Christ. This whole psalm commends with the utmost earnestness the grace of God, which is given freely.
*Be thou unto me a God, a protector, and a place of strength,* etc. Two things he promised, two others he renders.
*Of the sinner.* ((AUG.)) There are two kinds of sinners: some received the law, as the Jews and the Christians; others did not, as the pagans.

*From my youth.* ((CAS.)) That is, from my conversion, or from the time when I began to fight against the devil. ((AUG.)) *From my youth,* from the time when I began to hope in thee, etc., *as far as* a young man fights, but falls, unless God be his hope.

notes.text: Though I speak with all the tongues — Which are upon earth, and with the eloquence of an angel. And have not love - The love of God, and of all mankind for his sake, I am no better before God than the sounding instruments of brass, used in the worship of some of the heathen gods. Or a tinkling cymbal - This was made of two pieces of hollow brass, which, being struck together, made a tinkling, but very little variety of sound.

And though I have the gift of prophecy — Of foretelling future events. And understand all the mysteries - Both of God's word and providence. And all knowledge - Of things divine and human, that ever any mortal attained to. And though I have the highest degree of miracle working faith, and have not this love, I am nothing.

And though I — Deliberately, piece by piece. Give all my goods to feed the poor, yea, though I deliver up my body to be burned - Rather than I would renounce my religion. And have not the love - Hereafter described. It profiteth me nothing - Without this, whatever I speak, whatever I have, whatever I know, whatever I do, whatever I suffer, is nothing.

The love of God, and of our neighbour for God's sake, is patient toward, all men. It, suffers all the weakness, ignorance, errors, and infirmities of the children of God; all the malice and wickedness of the children of the world: and all this, not only for a time, but to the end. And in every step toward overcoming evil with good, it is kind, soft, mild, benign. It inspires the sufferer at once with the most amiable sweetness, and the most fervent and tender affection. Love acteth not rashly — Does not hastily condemn any one; never passes a severe sentence on a slight or sudden view of things. Nor does it ever act or behave in a violent, headstrong, or precipitate manner. Is not puffed up - Yea, humbles the soul to the dust.

It doth not behave indecently — Is not rude, or willingly offensive, to any. It renders to all their due - Suitable to time, person, and all other circumstances. Seeketh not her own - Ease, pleasure, honour, or temporal advantage. Nay, sometimes the lover of mankind seeketh not, in some sense, even his own spiritual advantage; does not think of himself, so long as a zeal for the glory of God and the souls of men swallows him up. But, though he is all on fire for these ends, yet he is not provoked to sharpness or unkindness toward any one. Outward provocations indeed will frequently occur; but he triumphs over all. Love thinketh no evil - Indeed it cannot but see and hear evil things, and know that they are so; but it does not willingly think evil of any; neither infer evil where it does not appear. It tears up, root and branch, all imagining of what we have not proof. It casts out all jealousies, all evil surmises, all readiness to believe evil.

Rejoiceth not in iniquity — Yea, weeps at either the sin or folly of even an enemy; takes no pleasure in hearing or in repeating it, but desires it may be forgotten forever. But rejoiceth in the truth - Bringing forth its proper fruit, holiness of heart and life. Good in general is its glory and joy, wherever diffused in all the world.

Love covereth all things — Whatever evil the lover of mankind sees, hears, or knows of any one, he mentions it to none; it never goes out of his lips, unless where absolute duty constrains to speak. Believeth all things - Puts the most favourable construction on everything, and is ever ready to believe whatever may tend to the advantage of any one character. And when it can no longer believe well, it hopes whatever may excuse or extenuate the fault which cannot be denied. Where it cannot even excuse, it hopes God will at length give repentance unto life. Meantime it endureth all things - Whatever the injustice, the malice, the cruelty of men can inflict. He can not only do, but likewise suffer, all things, through Christ who strengtheneth him.

Love never faileth — It accompanies to, and adorns us in, eternity; it prepares us for, and constitutes, heaven. But whether there be prophecies, they shall fail - When all things are fulfilled, and God is all in all. Whether there be tongues, they shall cease - One language shall prevail among all the inhabitants of heaven, and the low and imperfect languages of earth be forgotten. The knowledge likewise which we now so eagerly pursue, shall then vanish away - As starlight is lost in that of the midday sun, so our present knowledge in the light of eternity.

For we know in part, and we prophesy in part — The wisest of men have here but short, narrow, imperfect conceptions, even of the things round about them, and much more of the deep things of God. And even the prophecies which men deliver from God are far from taking in the whole of future events, or of that wisdom and knowledge of God which is treasured up in the scripture Revelation.

But when that which is perfect is come — At death and in the last day. That which is in part shall vanish away - Both that poor, low, imperfect, glimmering light, which is all the knowledge we now can attain to; and these slow and unsatisfactory methods of attaining, as well as of imparting it to others.
In our present state we are mere infants in point of knowledge, compared to what we shall be hereafter. I put away childish things — Of my own accord, willingly, without trouble.

Now we see — Even the things that surround us. But by means of a glass - Or mirror, which reflects only their imperfect forms, in a dim, faint, obscure manner; so that our thoughts about them are puzzling and intricate, and everything is a kind of riddle to us. But then - We shall see, not a faint reflection, but the objects themselves. Face to face - Distinctly. Now I know in part - Even when God himself reveals things to me, great part of them is still kept under the veil. But then I shall know even as also I am known - In a clear, full, comprehensive manner; in some measure like God, who penetrates the center of every object, and sees at one glance through my soul and all things.
Faith, hope, love — Are the sum of perfection on earth; love alone is the sum of perfection in heaven.

glossa.text: *If I speak with tongues,* etc. Here he proves that charity is the more excellent: because the others without it avail nothing, and it without them profits very much. *But charity.* Charity is the proper and singular fountain of good things, in which a stranger has no share. Which, like oil, cannot be pressed down to the bottom, but rises above; which, if it be lacking, the rest are had in vain: if it be present, all things are had? *As sounding brass,* etc. As brass resounds by some striking and not of itself, so he who speaks with tongues does so not of himself, who knows not what he speaks, but by the power of the Spirit brings forth things wherewith he may soothe his hearers.

*And if I should have prophecy.* As Balaam, and Caiaphas, and Saul. *I should know mysteries.* As Judas also among the apostles, and the devil, who (as Ezechiel says) knew the divine mysteries. *Knowledge.* As the scribes and the Pharisees, whence: *You have the key of knowledge, but neither do you enter in, nor do you suffer others to enter in ((Matth. XXIII))*. The wicked too assuredly have these things, who will also confess them in the judgment, where they will not dare to lie: to whom it will not be said, You have not had them, but *I have not known you:* because they had them without charity.

*Charity is patient,* etc. These are the arms wherewith the soldier of Christ is armed. Of which armour he has set foremost, as the chief arms, patience and kindness.

((ORIG.)) Patience, with an even mind, bears the evils brought upon it by its neighbours, kindness lovingly lays out its own goods upon its neighbours. *It is not envious.* Because another's good fortune does not sadden it. *It is not puffed up.* Because its own good fortune does not lift it up.
*It seeks not,* etc. It is no lover of money.

*It believes all things.* He does not say, it believes all men, because it believes God alone. *It hopes all things.* So it appeared in the fathers, that is, in the people of Israel, who hoped to have what God was promising. *It endures all things.* In the head, that is, in Christ, who patiently awaited the glory of the resurrection and of the ascension.

*Charity.* Again, in this it is the worthier, because it is ended neither in this world nor in the world to come, even though certain of its works cease. *It never falls away.* If by believing and hoping we love what is not yet seen, how much more when it shall be seen?
*That which is in part shall be done away.* It is the destruction of imperfection, when that which is imperfect is fulfilled in the whole.

*Now.* The images of the truth are seen through faith. *But then face to face.* That is, the things themselves will be seen manifestly. *Then I shall know.* That is, I shall see the things promised, *as he himself is,* which is to be present with God, where Christ is. Or, as I have been foreknown to know that which now is secret, *A glass.* It is the soul: a glass by whose power we in some manner know God, but darkly. *An enigma.* Now an enigma is not every allegory, but an obscure one. Whence, as by the glass he signified an image, so by the name of enigma he understands a likeness, albeit an obscure one and hard to perceive.

*Faith, hope,* etc. Which knowledge and prophecy serve as soldiers, without which the life of no just man is perfect. *But the greater of these is charity.* Charity is that to which here faith and hope cannot be lacking, but faith and hope can be without charity.

notes.text: Today is this scripture fulfilled in your ears — By what you hear me speak.

The gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth — A person of spiritual discernment may find in all the discourses of our Lord a peculiar sweetness, gravity, and becomingness, such as is not to be found in the same degree, not even in those of the apostles.

Ye will surely say — That is, your approbation now outweighs your prejudices. But it will not be so long. You will soon ask, why my love does not begin at home? Why I do not work miracles here, rather than at Capernaum? It is because of your unbelief. Nor is it any new thing for me to be despised in my own country. So were both Elijah and Elisha, and thereby driven to work miracles among heathens, rather than in Israel.

No prophet is acceptable in his own country — That is, in his own neighbourhood. It generally holds, that a teacher sent from God is not so acceptable to his neighbours as he is to strangers. The meanness of his family, or lowness of his circumstances, bring his office into contempt: nor can they suffer that he, who was before equal with, or below themselves, should now bear a superior character.

When the heaven was shut up three years and six months — Such a proof had they that God had sent him. In 1 Kings xviii, 1, it is said, The word of the Lord came to Elijah in the third year: namely, reckoning not from the beginning of the drought, but from the time when he began to sojourn with the widow of Sarepta. A year of drought had preceded this, while he dwelt at the brook Cherith. So that the whole time of the drought was (as St. James likewise observes) three years and six months. 1 Kings xvii, 19; xviii, 44.
2 Kings v, 14.

And all in the synagogue were filled with fury — Perceiving the purport of his discourse, namely, that the blessing which they despised, would be offered to, and accepted by, the Gentiles. So changeable are the hearts of wicked men! So little are their starts of love to be depended on! So unable are they to bear the close application, even of a discourse which they most admire!
Passing through the midst of them — Perhaps invisibly; or perhaps they were overawed; so that though they saw, they could not touch him.

glossa.text: *Physician.* As [they call him] the son of a carpenter, so by the same madness of error; they call him a physician, but in their error the truth lies hidden. For he was truly the son of a carpenter: of one who through him made all things in the beginning, who works in the Holy Ghost and in fire, who in the great house of this world makes vessels of diverse kinds. He is a physician also, because through him all things that are in the heavens and that are on earth have been restored. Who says of himself: *They that are in health need not a physician, but they that are ill ((Matth. IX))*.
*Amen I say to you. ((BEDA.))* Not only the Lord and head of the prophets, etc., *as far as* he turned away the miracles of his power.
*In the days of Elias. ((ID.))* As if he should say: It is not contrary to the example of the prophets, etc., *as far as* because there was no abundance for the knowing of the Godhead.
*A widow. ((ID.))* The widow to whom Elias is sent figures the Church of the Gentiles, etc., *as far as* in which the bread of eternal life is prepared for us.

*Naaman the Syrian. ((ID.))* Naaman, who is interpreted comeliness, signifies the people of the nations, etc., *as far as* because it behoves the baptized to be confirmed by partaking of the Lord's body.
*And they led him. ((ID.))* The Jews, worse disciples, with the devil for their master, etc., *as far as* they are preserved as though shaped by the hand of the divine Sculptor.

What a fellowship, what a joy divine
A mighty fortress is our God
A mighty fortress is our God

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Praise him with loud cymbals! Praise him with resounding cymbals!
echoes.note: The 'clanging cymbal' (kymbalon alalazon) draws on the temple cymbals of the psalm's call to praise God with 'loud clashing cymbals.' Paul ironically inverts liturgical worship: cymbals were sanctioned only as accompaniment to true praise, so love-less ecstatic speech is mere noise, the percussion without the worship. Verbal and conceptual links give this high volume.

echoes.text: David spoke to the chief of the Levites to appoint their brothers the singers, with instruments of music, stringed instruments and harps and cymbals, sounding aloud and lifting up the voice with joy.
echoes.note: David appoints Levites with instruments, including cymbals, to raise sounds of joy in temple worship. Paul's 'clanging cymbal' presupposes this fixed liturgical role of the cymbal in Israelite praise; without love the sound is emptied of its cultic meaning. Recurrence of the cymbal across the Chronicler strengthens availability.

echoes.text: So the singers, Heman, Asaph, and Ethan, were given cymbals of brass to sound aloud;
echoes.note: Heman, Asaph, and Ethan sound bronze cymbals; the noun chalkos/'bronze' resonates with Paul's 'sounding brass' (chalkos echon). The pairing of brass and cymbal in one verse-pair (sounding brass, clanging cymbal) mirrors the Chronicler's pairing of bronze cymbals in temple music, though the link is faint.

echoes.text: Thus all Israel brought up the ark of the covenant of Yahweh with shouting, and with sound of the cornet, and with trumpets, and with cymbals, sounding aloud with stringed instruments and harps.
echoes.note: All Israel brings up the ark with the sound of cymbals amid shouting (the verb cognate to alalazo). Paul's alalazon ('clanging') echoes the loud cultic shout/cymbal-clash of Israel's processional worship, here drained of substance when love is absent.

echoes.text: For you have made him a little lower than God, and crowned him with glory and honor.
echoes.note: 'Tongues of angels' presupposes the OT picture of angels (here 'a little lower than the angels/elohim') as a class of glorious heavenly beings whose speech surpasses human. The motif of angelic language is developed in Second-Temple texts; the canonical seedbed is the angelic praise tradition.

echoes.text: [source text not in the World English Bible]
echoes.note: Job's daughters receive cords enabling them to speak 'the dialect of angels' in hymnic praise. This pseudepigraphon attests the precise Second-Temple notion of distinct 'tongues of angels' that Paul invokes, supplying availability for his otherwise unparalleled phrase. Cited as cultural background, not a quoted source.

echoes.text: Who are you, great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you are a plain; and he will bring out the capstone with shouts of ‘Grace, grace, to it!’”
echoes.note: 'So as to remove mountains' echoes the oracle to Zerubbabel, 'Who are you, O great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you shall become a plain,' where the mountain of obstacle is leveled not by might but by God's Spirit. The mountain-as-impediment removed by divine power coheres with Paul's faith that 'removes mountains.' Volume is moderate; the saying also circulated in dominical tradition.

echoes.text: but there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets, and he has made known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Your dream, and the visions of your head on your bed, are these:
echoes.note: 'Know all mysteries and all knowledge' draws on Daniel's 'God in heaven who reveals mysteries,' the Aramaic raze that becomes the technical term for apocalyptic secrets. Paul's pairing of mysteries with prophetic gift coheres with Daniel's revealer-of-secrets, the principal OT source for the mystery-vocabulary.

echoes.text: Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low. The uneven shall be made level, and the rough places a plain.
echoes.note: 'Every mountain and hill shall be made low' supplies the eschatological image of mountains brought down before the coming of God. Paul's hyperbole of faith leveling mountains coheres with this prophetic flattening of obstacles, though the link is thematic rather than verbal.

echoes.text: You saw until a stone was cut out without hands, which struck the image on its feet that were of iron and clay, and broke them in pieces. Then was the iron, the clay, the brass, the silver, and the gold, broken in pieces together, and became like the chaff of the summer threshing floors; and the wind carried them away, so that no place was found for them: and the stone that struck the image became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth.
echoes.note: The stone cut without hands shatters the image and becomes a great mountain; the chapter's idiom of mysteries (raza) revealed undergirds Paul's 'know all mysteries.' The mountain motif here is faint, but Daniel's apocalyptic disclosure of 'mysteries' is the strongest OT seedbed for Paul's mysteria language.

echoes.text: Then was Nebuchadnezzar full of fury, and the form of his appearance was changed against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. He spoke, and commanded that they should heat the furnace seven times more than it was usually heated. He commanded certain mighty men who were in his army to bind Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, and to cast them into the burning fiery furnace. Then these men were bound in their pants, their tunics, and their mantles, and their other […]
echoes.note: 'Give my body to be burned' evokes Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego handing over their bodies to the fiery furnace rather than worship the image. The willing surrender of the body to flames as the supreme act of devotion supplies the model Paul deems worthless without love. Strong thematic coherence with martyr-by-fire piety.

echoes.text: And when he was utterly maimed, the king commanded to bring him to the fire, being yet alive, and to fry him in the pan. And as the vapor of the pan spread far, they and their mother also exhorted one another to die nobly, saying thus:
echoes.note: The seven brothers are tortured and burned in pans for refusing apostasy, the paradigmatic deuterocanonical martyrdom by fire. Paul's 'give my body to be burned' coheres with this celebrated martyr-narrative of bodily immolation, a readily available exemplum in his milieu. Volume moderate, recurrence high in martyr tradition.

echoes.text: Nebuchadnezzar spoke and said, Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who has sent his angel, and delivered his servants who trusted in him, and have changed the king’s word, and have yielded their bodies, that they might not serve nor worship any god, except their own God.
echoes.note: The king praises the three who 'yielded up their bodies' rather than serve any god but their own; the LXX phrasing of surrendering the body parallels Paul's paradoso to soma mou. This sharpens the furnace allusion: bodily self-surrender is praiseworthy, yet Paul says even this profits nothing without love.

echoes.text: so, Eleazar, the descendant of Aaron, wasted away by the fire, did not give up his reasoning.
echoes.note: Eleazar likened to one consumed by fire yet conquering through reason and piety; the pseudepigraphal celebration of burning martyrdom as the height of virtue reinforces the cultural availability of Paul's burnt-body topos. Cited as background to the burning-as-supreme-sacrifice motif.

echoes.text: He who has a generous eye will be blessed; for he shares his food with the poor.
echoes.note: 'Dole out all my goods to feed the poor' resonates with the OT praise of the one who shares bread with the poor and is blessed. Paul concedes the highest almsgiving, yet subordinates it to love; the link to the wisdom ideal of generosity to the poor is thematic and faint.

echoes.text: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,
echoes.note: 'Love is patient' (makrothymei) and 'kind' renders the LXX self-description of the LORD as 'slow to anger (makrothymos) and abounding in steadfast love.' Paul transposes the covenant attributes of God's character onto agape, so that the hymn portrays love with the very predicates of the divine name. High volume, strong coherence: the Exodus formula is the foundational OT portrait of patient, faithful love.

echoes.text: Yahweh is gracious, merciful, slow to anger, and of great loving kindness.
echoes.note: 'The LORD is gracious and merciful, slow to anger and great in steadfast love' restates the Exodus formula and grounds Paul's 'love is patient and kind.' Its liturgical recurrence (Pss 86:15; 103:8; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2) gives the patient-and-kind pairing strong availability and volume as a fixed description of covenant love.

echoes.text: Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all wrongs.
echoes.note: 'Love covers all offenses' (versus hatred that stirs strife) underwrites Paul's 'love takes no account of evil' and 'bears all things.' The proverb's antithesis of love that overlooks wrongs against hate that provokes maps directly onto Paul's list of what love is not (provoked, resentful). The covering/non-reckoning of evil is a strong conceptual parallel.

echoes.text: and let none of you devise evil in your hearts against his neighbor, and love no false oath: for all these are things that I hate,” says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Do not devise evil in your hearts against one another... for all these things I hate' coheres with 'love takes no account of evil' and 'does not rejoice in unrighteousness.' Zechariah pairs the rejection of inward malice with truth-telling (8:16), matching Paul's contrast of evil-plotting against rejoicing in the truth.

echoes.text: He who covers an offense promotes love; but he who repeats a matter separates best friends.
echoes.note: 'Whoever covers an offense seeks love, but he who repeats a matter separates friends' parallels love that 'takes no account of evil' and 'bears all things.' The wisdom ideal of not rehearsing wrongs is a close conceptual match for Paul's non-reckoning love, reinforcing the Prov 10:12 covering-motif.

echoes.text: Blessed is the man to whom Yahweh doesn’t impute iniquity, in whose spirit there is no deceit.
echoes.note: 'Blessed is the one to whom the LORD imputes no iniquity' supplies the accounting idiom behind 'love takes no account of evil' (ou logizetai to kakon). Just as God's blessing rests on not-reckoning sin, Paul's love refuses to keep a ledger of wrongs; the logizomai/non-imputation link gives moderate verbal warrant.

echoes.text: He who is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who has a quick temper displays folly.
echoes.note: 'Whoever is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who is hasty of spirit exalts folly' coheres with love that 'is not provoked' (ou paroxynetai). The wisdom valorization of slow anger against quick temper supports Paul's portrait, though without specific verbal contact.

echoes.text: Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.
echoes.note: 'Pride goes before destruction, a haughty spirit before a fall' undergirds love that 'doesn't brag, is not proud' (ou physioutai). The wisdom condemnation of arrogance is the broad OT seedbed for Paul's anti-boasting predicates, a thematic rather than verbal echo.

echoes.text: For she that is the architect of all things taught me, even wisdom. For there is in her a spirit quick of understanding, holy, Alone in kind, manifold, Subtil, freely moving, Clear in utterance, unpolluted, Distinct, unharmed, Loving what is good, keen, unhindered, Beneficent, loving toward man, Stedfast, sure, free from care, All-powerful, all-surveying, And penetrating through all spirits That are quick of understanding, pure, most subtle: For wisdom is […]
echoes.note: The hymn to Wisdom enumerates her attributes (kindly, loving the good, beneficent, unhindered) in a rhetorical catalogue strikingly like Paul's catalogue of love's attributes. As a Second-Temple model of personified virtue praised by predicate-lists, it offers availability for the form and ethos of Paul's encomium to agape.

echoes.text: Be not angry with your neighbor for every wrong; And do nothing by works of violence. Pride is hateful before the Lord and before men; And in the judgement of both will unrighteousness err. Sovereignty is transferred from nation to nation, Because of iniquities, and deeds of violence, and greed of money.
echoes.note: Ben Sira warns against bearing a grudge, against arrogance, and against the insolence (hyperephania) that God hates. The cluster of grudge-bearing, pride, and rude insolence parallels Paul's love that is 'not proud,' 'doesn't behave inappropriately,' and 'resentful,' giving deuterocanonical wisdom support for the vice-list love negates.

echoes.text: Don’t rejoice when your enemy falls. Don’t let your heart be glad when he is overthrown;
echoes.note: 'Do not rejoice when your enemy falls' parallels love that 'doesn't rejoice in unrighteousness.' The wisdom prohibition of malicious joy at another's wrong/downfall is a close conceptual match for Paul's chairei... ou epi te adikia, supporting the contrast with rejoicing in the truth.

echoes.text: Behold, you desire truth in the inward parts. You teach me wisdom in the inmost place.
echoes.note: 'You delight in truth in the inward being' resonates with love that 'rejoices with the truth' (synchairei te aletheia). The OT pairing of God's delight in truth over against iniquity supports Paul's antithesis of unrighteousness and truth, though the verbal contact is loose.

echoes.text: Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all wrongs.
echoes.note: 'Bears all things' (panta stegei) reprises the love-covers-all-offenses motif: stego ('cover/bear in silence') overlaps with the proverb's love that covers transgressions. The recurrence of the covering-language across 13:5 and 13:7 strengthens the link to the Proverbs source for love's forbearance.

echoes.text: It is good that a man should hope and quietly wait for the salvation of Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'It is good to wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD' coheres with love that 'hopes all things, endures all things' (panta hypomenei). The OT ideal of patient, hopeful endurance under affliction supplies the disposition Paul ascribes to love, a thematic echo of waiting-hope.

echoes.text: Wait for Yahweh. Be strong, and let your heart take courage. Yes, wait for Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Wait for the LORD; be strong, and let your heart take courage' parallels love that 'hopes all things, endures all things.' The recurring OT summons to hopeful endurance and waiting on God undergirds Paul's panta elpizei, panta hypomenei as the posture of covenant trust.

echoes.text: With him, I will speak mouth to mouth, even plainly, and not in riddles; and he shall see Yahweh’s form. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant, against Moses?”
echoes.note: 'Then face to face' draws on the LORD speaking with Moses 'mouth to mouth, clearly and not in dark speech (di' ainigmaton)'; Paul's 'in a mirror, dimly (en ainigmati)' uses the very LXX word from Numbers. The contrast of riddling/indirect sight now versus direct, unmediated vision then is grounded precisely in the Mosaic prerogative. High volume by the shared ainigma term.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. He turned again into the camp, but his servant Joshua, the son of Nun, a young man, didn’t depart from the Tent.
echoes.note: 'The LORD used to speak to Moses face to face (prosopon kata prosopon), as one speaks to a friend' supplies Paul's exact phrase 'face to face' for the eschatological vision. The Mosaic privilege of direct divine encounter becomes the eschatological norm Paul anticipates, a strong verbal and conceptual link.

echoes.text: Yahweh, you have searched me, and you know me. You know my sitting down and my rising up. You perceive my thoughts from afar. You search out my path and my lying down, and are acquainted with all my ways. For there is not a word on my tongue, but, behold, Yahweh, you know it altogether. You hem me in behind and before. You laid your hand on me. This knowledge is beyond me. It’s lofty. I can’t attain it.
echoes.note: 'Then I will know fully, even as I was also fully known' echoes the psalmist's confession that the LORD has searched and known him completely, his sitting and rising, his thoughts and ways, a knowledge 'too wonderful' to attain. Paul's epignosomai kathos kai epegnosthen inverts the asymmetry: now God knows me fully; then I will know likewise. Strong coherence with the OT theme of being exhaustively known by God.

echoes.text: Since then, there has not arisen a prophet in Israel like Moses, whom Yahweh knew face to face,
echoes.note: 'No prophet has arisen since like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face' reinforces the face-to-face idiom as the unique mode of unmediated knowledge of God. Paul universalizes this Mosaic singularity to all believers 'then,' so the prophetic incompleteness of 13:9 yields to Mosaic immediacy.

echoes.text: Jacob called the name of the place Peniel: for, he said, “I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved.”
echoes.note: Jacob names Peniel, 'for I have seen God face to face (eidon... prosopon pros prosopon), and yet my life is preserved.' The patriarchal precedent of surviving a face-to-face vision of God feeds the OT 'face to face' tradition Paul invokes for final beatific sight. Recurrence of the idiom across Genesis-Deuteronomy strengthens availability.

echoes.text: “Before I formed you in the belly, I knew you. Before you came out of the womb, I sanctified you. I have appointed you a prophet to the nations.”
echoes.note: 'Before I formed you in the womb I knew you' contributes to the OT motif of God's prior, exhaustive knowledge of the person that underlies 'even as I was fully known' (epegnosthen). The divine foreknowing of the individual coheres with Paul's claim to be already fully known by God, a faint supporting echo.

echoes.text: For she is an effulgence from everlasting light, And an unspotted mirror of the working of God, And an image of his goodness.
echoes.note: Wisdom is 'a spotless mirror (esoptron) of the working of God.' Paul's 'we see in a mirror' (di' esoptrou) shares the rare mirror-as-medium-of-divine-knowledge image; the deuterocanonical sapiential mirror supplies availability for Paul's epistemological metaphor of indirect present sight.

echoes.text: “But where shall wisdom be found? Where is the place of understanding? Man doesn’t know its price; Neither is it found in the land of the living. The deep says, ‘It isn’t in me.’ The sea says, ‘It isn’t with me.’ It can’t be gotten for gold, neither shall silver be weighed for its price. It can’t be valued with the gold of Ophir, with the precious onyx, or the sapphire. Gold and glass can’t equal it, neither shall it be exchanged for jewels of fine gold. […]
echoes.note: 'Where shall wisdom be found?'—it is hidden, known fully only to God who sees the ends of the earth. The wisdom poem's contrast of human partial knowledge against God's complete knowing coheres with Paul's 'we know in part' giving way to full knowledge, a thematic echo of the limits of present human cognition.

echoes.text: Behold, his soul is puffed up. It is not upright in him, but the righteous will live by his faith.
echoes.note: 'The righteous shall live by his faith(fulness)' supplies the OT root of Paul's enduring 'faith' (pistis) in the triad faith-hope-love that 'remains.' The prophetic grounding of life in abiding faith coheres with Paul's claim that faith abides into the eschaton, a thematic rather than verbal echo.

echoes.text: He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?
echoes.note: 'To do justice, and to love kindness (chesed), and to walk humbly with your God' offers an OT triad of enduring religious requirements culminating in covenant love. The form of a compressed triad whose summit is love/chesed loosely anticipates Paul's faith-hope-love crowned by the greatest, love. Faint formal echo.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound; to proclaim the year of Yahweh’s favor, and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all who mourn;
echoes.note: The Nazareth scroll reading 'The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to preach good news to the poor... release to the captives... recovering of sight to the blind... to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord' is a formal citation of Isaiah 61:1-2 (LXX). Highest Volume in the chapter; explicitly introduced as 'the book of the prophet Isaiah.'
echoes.lxxText: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach glad tidings to the poor, to heal the broken in heart, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind; to declare the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of recompence; to comfort all that mourn;

echoes.text: “Isn’t this the fast that I have chosen: to release the bonds of wickedness, to undo the bands of the yoke, and to let the oppressed go free, and that you break every yoke?
echoes.note: The clause 'to deliver/set at liberty those who are crushed (oppressed)' is spliced in from Isaiah 58:6 (LXX 'aphesei tethrausmenous'), not part of Isa 61. The deliberate conflation of two 'release/aphesis' texts is a recognized Lukan composite citation; high Volume and verbatim LXX wording.

echoes.text: You shall make the fiftieth year holy, and proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee to you; and each of you shall return to his own property, and each of you shall return to his family.
echoes.note: 'To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord' and 'release/aphesis' evoke the Jubilee of Leviticus 25, when liberty is proclaimed and debts/captives released. Isaiah 61 itself draws on Jubilee language; Luke makes the year-of-release motif programmatic, giving strong Coherence and Availability.

echoes.text: to open the blind eyes, to bring the prisoners out of the dungeon, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison.
echoes.note: 'Recovering of sight to the blind' and 'release to the captives' resonate with the Servant's task in Isaiah 42:7 ('to open blind eyes, to bring out prisoners'). Recurrence of the Isaianic Servant/blindness motif strengthens this, though the wording is closest to Isa 61/LXX.

echoes.text: In that day, the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see out of obscurity and out of darkness.
echoes.note: The opening of blind eyes and hearing of the deaf in Isaiah 29:18 belongs to the cluster of Isaianic restoration texts Luke draws on for sight-to-the-blind. Faint and secondary to Isa 61, but coherent with Luke's Isaianic program.

echoes.text: You are the most excellent of the sons of men. Grace has anointed your lips, therefore God has blessed you forever.
echoes.note: The crowd's wonder at the 'gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth' faintly echoes Psalm 45:2 (LXX 44:3), 'grace is poured upon your lips.' Low Volume; the verbal overlap (grace + mouth/lips) is suggestive but the connection is contested.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says Yahweh concerning the men of Anathoth, who seek your life, saying, You shall not prophesy in Yahweh’s name, that you not die by our hand;
echoes.note: 'No prophet is acceptable in his hometown,' and the townsmen's coming murderous rejection, reflects the prophet-rejected-by-his-own pattern, e.g. Jeremiah's own people of Anathoth seeking his life (Jer 11:21). Faint, pattern-level allusion rather than verbal citation.

echoes.text: Elijah the Tishbite, who was of the foreigners of Gilead, said to Ahab, “As Yahweh, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word.”
echoes.note: 'When the sky was shut up three years and six months... a great famine' summarizes Elijah's drought announced in 1 Kings 17:1 (and ended in 18:1). Jesus names the era explicitly ('in the days of Elijah'); high Volume narrative citation.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s word came to him, saying, “Arise, go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and stay there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to sustain you.” So he arose and went to Zarephath; and when he came to the gate of the city, behold, a widow was there gathering sticks: and he called to her, and said, “Please get me a little water in a vessel, that I may drink.” As she was going to get it, he called to her, and said, “Please bring me a morsel of […]
echoes.note: 'Elijah was sent... to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow' directly retells 1 Kings 17:8-16, the widow of Zarephath. Explicit naming of place and figure makes this a high-Volume citation deployed as Gentile-inclusion precedent.

echoes.text: Now Naaman, captain of the army of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master, and honorable, because by him Yahweh had given victory to Syria: he was also a mighty man of valor, but he was a leper. The Syrians had gone out in bands, and had brought away captive out of the land of Israel a little maiden; and she waited on Naaman’s wife. She said to her mistress, “I wish that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria! Then he would heal him […]
echoes.note: 'Naaman, the Syrian' cleansed of leprosy by Elisha retells 2 Kings 5:1-14. Named figure and event; high Volume, paired with the Zarephath widow to ground Jesus' point that prophets are sent to Gentiles when Israel rejects them.

echoes.text: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”
echoes.note: The synagogue's murderous rage and attempt to throw Jesus off the cliff continues the rejected-prophet motif (cf. Israel killing the prophets, 1 Kings 19:10,14). Pattern-level echo reinforcing the Elijah framing just invoked; faint verbal contact.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Before I formed you in the womb I knew you.
In you, O Lord, we take refuge.
Do not be afraid, for I am with you to deliver you.
In you, O Lord, we take refuge.
And now faith, hope, and love abide; the greatest of these is love.
Come, let us worship. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Hear the word spoken to a young and frightened prophet: I knew you before you were.
In you, O Lord, we take refuge.
Do not say you are too young, too small, too unready; I will put my words in your mouth.
In you, O Lord, we take refuge.
The truth is not always welcome; even hometowns turn on the ones who tell it.
In you, O Lord, we take refuge.
But love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.
In you, O Lord, we take refuge; love never ends!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: Before you were formed, God knew you and called you.
In you, O Lord, we take refuge.
Do not be afraid; God puts his words in your mouth.
In you, O Lord, we take refuge.
Love bears, believes, hopes, endures; love never ends.
In you, O Lord, we take refuge. Amen.
